newsitem.title: UK: C&W might fight U.S. bid to cut call prices.
newsitem.headline: C&W might fight U.S. bid to cut call prices.

text.p: Cable and Wireless (C&W), Britain's second largest telecommunications company, said on Friday it was considering an appeal to a decision by America's top telecoms regulator to slash the price U.S. carriers pay their overseas counterparts for delivering calls.

C&W said it was seeking legal advice to see whether it could challenge a decision by America's Federal Communications Commission (FCC) that will cut the average price of international calls from the U.S. to 20 cents per minute from 88 cents, over five years.
"(An appeal) must be an option and our lawyers will be looking at it," John Taylor, C&W's director of group regulatory affairs, told Reuters.

U.S. carriers paid about $5.4 billion more than they were paid by foreign carriers to complete calls in 1996, reflecting both the high costs of overseas carriers and the large immigrant population in the U.S.

The FCC proposed an order setting benchmarks of 15 to 23 cents per minute for international calls to reduce the so-called "settlement" rates that U.S. telecoms companies pay foreign groups to complete U.S.-originated calls.
The benchmarks are sharply below the level many overseas telephone companies charge for delivering U.S. calls.
The decision, following a draft published in December, has fuelled anger at the unilateral way the FCC is acting.

"This attempt by the FCC to deal with the issue of accounting rates unilaterally will not be in the interests of all customers or all operators around the world and risks undermining the very existence of international telecoms services," Taylor said.
C&W says any such decision should be taken by the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) in Geneva.
While accounting rates on the busy transatlantic U.S and British route are already around 15 cents per minute, those in developing countries are much higher.

Taylor, who said poorer nations might have to reduce rates from as much as 100 cents to 23 cents per minute, noted that developing countries rely on these vital hard currency revenues which often come from the U.S.
The FCC decision affects only bi-lateral routes from America, but it could have a severe knock-on effect as operators could be encouraged to refile their international traffic through the U.S..

C&W lawyers will have to wait to see the exact terms of the FCC order, which are expected to be published early next week, before advising C&W either to challenge the decision or to ask for the FCC to reconsider.
British Telecommunications Plc, the country's biggest carrier, however, said it welcomed any move that would ensure that telephone call prices reflect more closely the cost of delivering them.
